title: POC scoping: success criteria signoff & acceptance tests
summary: Redwood and Orchid align on POC success criteria, benchmark plan, workload sizing, and timelines. Key acceptance tests include latency p95/p99 targets, throughput goals, semantic accuracy thresholds for embeddings and generation, hallucination rate limits, and cost targets. Next steps: Redwood to deliver benchmark plan and SOW; Orchid to share sample dataset and prompt sets; schedule infrastructure kickoff and 2-week pilot start window.
topics: Workload sizing and synthetic load profile
next_steps: Redwood to send benchmark plan + SOW by 2025-02-17
Orchid to share 1,000 sample prompts, 2k sample records and access to test dataset by 2025-02-12
Schedule infra kickoff (Carlos + Daniel) week of 2025-02-17

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-02-10
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Kim (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Orchid - Head of ML), Carlos Ruiz (Orchid - Infra), Lena Zhou (Orchid - PM)
Recording ID: ff-20250210-orchid-poc-001

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy): discuss success criteria and acceptance tests, agree on benchmarks and timeline, next steps include SOW and data share.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Sarah Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to use this hour to lock down the POC acceptance criteria and the benchmarks we'll run. um, main goals are to make sure we have clear go/no-go thresholds and reporting.
[00:18] Maya Patel: thanks Sarah, yeah on our side we need to know latency, throughput, cost and also model quality measures — like hallucination rate and semantic recall for embeddings.
[00:32] Daniel Park: totally, we'll propose a suite of tests. typically we run three buckets: latency/throughput under realistic traffic, quality evals against your golden set, and stability under sustained load.
[00:46] Carlos Ruiz: quick infra note — we will want VPC peering for the private pilot, or at least a secure test path. and we need to understand peak concurrency to size the Dedicated pool.
[01:02] Sarah Kim: good point. Carlos, can you share a short concurrency profile? like average rps and peak rps over a 1-hour window?
[01:10] Carlos Ruiz: yes i can, offhand right now typical is ~5 rps average, peak of 45 rps for spikes, with p50 request size about 350 tokens, p95 about 1,200 tokens.
[01:26] Daniel Park: perfect that's helpful. for the POC we'll size the synthetic load to emulate your peak: target throughput 40 rps sustained for 10 minutes in one stage, and ramp tests up to 60 rps to see autoscaling behavior.
[01:42] Lena Zhou: can you also capture cost metrics? we want per-1M-token cost estimates for hosted vs dedicated during the pilot.
[01:50] Sarah Kim: yes we'll report tokenized usage and unit cost. decision criteria should include a cost delta threshold, e.g., if Dedicated doesn't get us at least 20% reduction in per-token cost at expected load, then we revisit.
[02:03] Maya Patel: on quality — for our retrieval/assistant flows we need embed recall @k=10 to be within 2% of our on-prem baseline, and generation answer accuracy (exact match or F1 depending on task) to be within 3 points. hallucination rate should be under 1% on our curated test set.
[02:21] Daniel Park: makes sense. we'll run similarity evaluations for embeddings (cosine/ann index) and generation evals with your golden answers. we'll compute EM/F1 and an automated hallucination detector, plus human spot-checks on a sample of 100 responses.
[02:39] Carlos Ruiz: how long will the benchmark run take? i.e., when can we expect results?
[02:44] Sarah Kim: our typical cadence: week 0 (kickoff) — infra and data share; week 1 — run bench harness and short functional tests; week 2 — sustained load and stability tests, and then 2-3 business days for analysis and reporting. overall about 2 weeks end-to-end for a pilot.
[03:02] Maya Patel: for acceptance the SPoF is: we need p95 latency below 400ms for generation requests at 256 token responses and p99 under 1s. Is that realistic?
[03:13] Daniel Park: p95 < 400ms at 256 tokens is aggressive but doable on Dedicated with optimizations and quantized models. we should set staged thresholds: p95 <= 400ms (target), p95 <= 600ms (acceptable), p99 <= 1s (target). we can also provide a fallback model that costs less but has higher latency if needed.
[03:30] Lena Zhou: and what about model variants — are we allowed to use quantized versions?
[03:34] Sarah Kim: yes quantization is in scope. Redwood recommends we test 8-bit and 4-bit variants for cost/latency tradeoffs. acceptance should allow quantized models as long as quality thresholds are met.
[03:45] Maya Patel: reporting format — we need a CSV plus dashboard. columns: test_name, model_variant, timestamp, rps, concurrency, p50, p95, p99, average_latency_ms, error_rate, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_estimate_usd. Also separate quality CSV for EM/F1/hallucination.
[04:03] Daniel Park: we'll produce the CSV and also a preliminary Redwood Console dashboard link. example CSV headers will match what you described. we'll also include raw logs (gzipped) for forensic analysis.
[04:16] Carlos Ruiz: security questions — we'll need audit logs and an SSO + RBAC story. Also encryption at rest with our KMS.
[04:25] Sarah Kim: yes, for a Private/Dedicated POC we can enable audit logs, SAML SSO and integrate with your KMS. we'll include a security checklist in the SOW.
[04:36] Maya Patel: what are go/no-go thresholds summarized so stakeholders can sign off?
[04:40] Sarah Kim: I'll propose a concise acceptance matrix. at a high level: 1) Latency/Throughput: p95 latency within target band and system can sustain expected throughput for a sustained window; 2) Quality: EM/F1 within agreed delta and hallucination <1%; 3) Cost: per-token estimate within agreed savings threshold for Dedicated; 4) Stability: no critical errors > 0.1% error rate during sustained tests; 5) Security: required controls in place. If all met, go. If one critical (quality or security) fails, no-go.
[05:09] Daniel Park: also recommend a small sample of manual QA signoffs: 10 stakeholders to check a randomized set of 50 responses, just to capture human judgement which detectors might miss.
[05:21] Lena Zhou: that seems fair. also who signs off on the success criteria from Orchid?
[05:25] Maya Patel: i'll be primary for model quality signoff, lena will sign for product fit, carlos on infra/security. final exec signoff will be me + CTO.
[05:36] Sarah Kim: great. i'll send an acceptance matrix and we can iterate.
[05:40] Carlos Ruiz: any dependencies from our side besides data and peering?
[05:44] Daniel Park: also we'll need a test account with tokenized usage or short-lived credentials to push load; and a list of whitelisted IPs for the bench if peering isn't possible initially.
[05:56] Maya Patel: one more thing — will Redwood provide a runbook for troubleshooting during the bench?
[06:00] Sarah Kim: yes, Daniel will supply a runbook and we'll schedule a standing 30-min daily check while the benchmark runs.
[06:08] Daniel Park: I'll also include a list of metrics we'll stream to your monitoring: request latencies, GPU utilization, queue lengths, KV cache hit rates, and per-model token accounting.
[06:20] Lena Zhou: timeline recap?
[06:22] Sarah Kim: Kickoff and infra setup by 2025-02-17, dataset and prompts by 2025-02-12, bench runs 2025-02-24 to 2025-03-03 (flexible), analysis/reporting by 2025-03-06, decision meeting week of 2025-03-10.
[06:40] Maya Patel: that timeline works for us.
[06:44] Sarah Kim: ok we'll send SOW, benchmark plan, CSV schema, and schedule the infra kickoff. any other open questions?
[06:52] Carlos Ruiz: none from infra.
[06:54] Lena Zhou: none here.
[06:56] Maya Patel: just ask that the hallucination detector thresholds be documented in the report.
[06:59] Daniel Park: noted, we'll include metric definitions and test harness code links in the deliverables.
[07:06] Sarah Kim: perfect. thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[07:10] End of recording.
